strengths: The row-block update is simple and preserves XᵀX exactly, providing a useful mechanism for optimization over rectangular Stiefel manifolds.
Reducing two-row subproblems to one-dimensional optimization, including both rotations and reflections, is a practically appealing approach to handling nonsmooth penalties without smoothing.

The experiments cover four optimization problems, ten datasets, several ranks and regularization strengths, and relevant baselines including ManPG and OptM. The reported results show substantial objective improvements in several settings.
weaknesses: The central stationarity equivalence in Theorem 5.5(c) is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix B.8 incorrectly exchanges 'for every block there exists a suitable subgradient' with existence of one subgradient satisfying every block. A counterexample uses s=1/√2, X=[[s,0],[1/2,s],[1/2,-s]], h(X)=||X||₁, and linear f with gradient [[-1,0],[-1/2,-1],[-1/2,1]]. Then ∂F(X) consists of G(t)=[[0,t],[1/2,0],[1/2,0]], |t|≤1. Stationarity of blocks (1,2) and (1,3) requires t=1/2 and t=-1/2 respectively, while block (2,3) is already stationary. Thus all two-row blocks are stationary but X is not critical. This directly undermines the advertised optimality hierarchy.

The strong-convergence proof has additional substantive errors. Equation (56), step ②, exchanges Bᵗ and Bᵗ⁺¹ inside an expectation involving Xᵗ⁺¹, although Xᵗ⁺¹ depends on Bᵗ. Lemma 6.6 confuses the root-mean-square block residual with its mean. Appendix B.13 applies the local KL inequality around a global minimizer without establishing proximity to that minimizer. Moreover, the bounded-subgradient assumption excludes the ℓ₀ penalty at zero and the nonnegativity indicator at boundary points. Theorem 6.8 therefore does not establish the claimed guarantees.

The supposedly exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Section 7.1 omits cos(θ)=0 from the tangent parametrization, gives xᵢ/yᵢ instead of -xᵢ/yᵢ for zero-crossing breakpoints, and incorrectly discards terms with yᵢ=0: their ℓ₁ contribution |xᵢ|/√(1+t²) still depends on t. These errors matter because the analysis requires globally solved subproblems. Section 7.2 also omits the proximal term required by Equation (11), disconnecting the described approximate solver from the analyzed algorithm.

The nonnegative initialization in Section 9.1 is infeasible as specified: setting X⁰(Gᵢ,i)=1/|Gᵢ| gives column squared norm 1/|Gᵢ|, whereas normalization requires 1/√|Gᵢ|. Since OBCD preserves the initial Gram matrix, this initialization cannot produce the reported orthogonality residuals. The manuscript needs to reconcile the implementation with its description.

The empirical comparisons lack controls needed to substantiate the efficiency and solution-quality claims. Only the proposed breakpoint routine receives C++ acceleration; repeated runs and uncertainty estimates are absent; and the additional ten-second OBCD refinement is not compared against continuing the baseline for the same additional budget. Improvements after refinement consequently do not establish stronger stationarity.

Evaluation and reproducibility remain incomplete despite the extensive tables. There is no direct comparison with the discussed Givens-coordinate methods or controlled ablation of reflections, the fifth-order solver, and block size. All experiments use k=2 and n≤1000, limiting evidence for scalability and generality. Baseline tuning, inner-solver tolerances, data-subset seeds, and a concrete reproducible code release are insufficiently documented.

strengths: The orthogonal row-update construction preserves XᵀX exactly and reduces each update to a small optimization problem, addressing an important class of learning objectives.
Considering both rotations and reflections, together with sampled greedy working-set selection, provides useful practical algorithmic ideas.

Experiments cover four problem families, ten datasets, multiple ranks and regularization settings, and relevant baselines including ManPG and OptM. Several reported objective improvements are substantial.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy in Theorem 5.5 is false under the stated assumptions. The proof confuses a potentially different subgradient for each block with one shared subgradient. A concrete counterexample uses a=1/√2, X=[[a,0],[a,0],[0,1]], h(X)=||X||₁, and f(X)=1.5(X₁₂−X₂₂)−X₁₁−X₂₁−X₃₂. Every two-row orthogonal update has F≥F(X)=0, making X exact block-2 stationary. Nevertheless, the feasible curve [[a,−a sin t],[a,a sin t],[0,cos t]] has F=−a sin t<0 for small positive t. Thus OBCD-Exact can stall at a noncritical point.

The strong convergence analysis contains additional substantive errors. Lemma 6.6(b) fails even for h=0, f(x)=x₂, x=e₁ on St(3,1), and k=2: its left-hand side equals 1, whereas its right-hand side equals √(2/3). Appendix B.11 incorrectly passes from a second-moment bound to a first-moment bound. Appendix B.10 also interchanges the previous and next sampled blocks despite the updated iterate depending on the previous block. These invalidate key ingredients of Theorem 6.8.

The inner solvers do not satisfy their advertised guarantees as written. The substitution t=tan θ omits cos θ=0, potentially excluding global minimizers. Removing coordinates with yᵢ=0 changes the ℓ₁ objective because |xᵢ|/√(1+t²) is not constant. The stated ℓ₀/ℓ₁ breakpoints also have an incorrect sign. Furthermore, Section 7.2 omits the proximal term required by subproblem (11). These issues undermine the claimed exactness and applicability of the descent analysis.

The nonnegative initialization in Section 9.1 uses 1/|Gᵢ|, giving each column squared norm 1/|Gᵢ| rather than 1. Orthogonal row updates preserve this error, so the written procedure cannot produce Table 5's near-machine-precision feasibility. This implementation-critical inconsistency requires correction and clarification.

The empirical comparisons need stronger controls and reproducibility details. OBCD alone uses a C++ breakpoint kernel, confounding runtime comparisons with implementation differences. Baseline tuning, inner stopping tolerances, data preprocessing, and variability across randomized runs are insufficiently documented. Testing only k=2 and n≤1000, primarily through short-budget best-observed objective gaps, does not establish the broader scalability or stronger-stationarity claims.

strengths: Addresses an important optimization setting with relevant applications to sparse PCA, nonnegative PCA, and nonlinear eigenvalue problems.
The row-block update preserves orthogonality through small orthogonal transformations. Including both rotations and reflections is useful for exploring both components of the square orthogonal group.

The experiments cover four problem families, ten datasets, and several ranks and regularization levels. The reported objective improvements and comparisons between random and greedy working-set selection suggest practical potential.
weaknesses: The central equivalence in Theorem 5.5(c) is false under the stated assumptions. Consider n=r=3, k=2, X=I, f(X)=<A,X>, A=[[0,-1/2,1/2],[1/2,0,-1/2],[-1/2,1/2,0]], and h(X)=sum_i |sum_j X_ij-1|. Every two-row subproblem is stationary at identity, but global criticality requires t1-t2=t2-t3=t3-t1=1 for subgradient coefficients ti in [-1,1], which is impossible. Appendix B.8 incorrectly converts separate, block-dependent subgradient choices into one common subgradient. This invalidates the claimed equivalence and the general interpretation of block stationarity as stronger than criticality.

The strong-convergence proof has additional substantive errors. Appendix B.10, equation (56), exchanges B^t and B^(t+1) even though X^(t+1) depends on B^t; identical sampling distributions do not justify this substitution. Lemma 6.6(b) is also false even for smooth objectives: n=r=3, k=2, X=I, f(X)=X_12, h=0 gives a left-hand side of sqrt(2) and a right-hand side of sqrt(2/3). The squared-norm calculation does not establish the asserted expected-norm bound. Consequently, Theorem 6.8 and the associated convergence-rate claims lack a valid foundation.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as specified in Section 7.1. The substitution t=tan(theta) omits cos(theta)=0, where a global minimizer can occur. Terms with y_i=0 cannot simply be deleted for the l1 penalty because lambda|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) still depends on t. Furthermore, zeros of x_i+t*y_i occur at -x_i/y_i, whereas the listed l0/l1 breakpoints use the opposite sign. These issues undermine the exact-minimization premise used by the theory.

The nonnegative-PCA initialization contradicts the reported feasibility. Section 9.1 sets X^0(G_i,i)=1/|G_i|, producing a Gram matrix with diagonal entries 1/|G_i| rather than 1. Since the proposed updates preserve that Gram matrix, they cannot produce Table 5's near-machine-precision orthogonality from this initialization. An additional normalization, normally 1/sqrt(|G_i|), must be specified and checked against the implementation.

The empirical efficiency and better-solution claims need stronger controls. Only OBCD's breakpoint routine uses C++, without an implementation-matched comparison. Hybrid methods receive an additional ten seconds without a corresponding control that continues the baseline for the same additional time. Repeated trials, variability, baseline tuning details, and comparisons at matched stationarity tolerances are absent. Improvement after additional computation does not establish that stronger stationarity caused the gain.

Positioning and reproducibility remain incomplete. Comparisons omit the cited Givens-coordinate approaches and recent exact-penalty methods for nonnegative orthogonality. Ablations do not isolate reflections, the fifth-order solver, or block sizes beyond k=2, and the tested feature dimensions are at most 1000. Data preprocessing, random seeds, nonlinear-eigenvalue instance construction, and a concrete versioned code release are insufficiently specified.

strengths: The row-block update preserves orthogonality exactly, handles rectangular Stiefel constraints, and includes both rotations and reflections.
The majorization construction supports sufficient decrease when subproblems are solved as required, while k=2 reduces each subproblem to one-dimensional optimization.
Experiments cover four problem classes, ten datasets, and multiple ranks and regularization settings, reporting substantial objective improvements in many cases against relevant baselines.
weaknesses: Theorem 5.5(c) is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix B.8 incorrectly exchanges 'for every block, there exists a subgradient' with existence of one subgradient satisfying every block. A counterexample uses h(X)=||X||_1, f(X)=<C,X>, C=[[-1,0],[-1.5,-1],[-1.5,1]], and X=[[s,0],[0.5,s],[0.5,-s]], where s=1/sqrt(2). This X is feasible and every two-row subproblem is critical at the identity, yet the minimum global residual ||G-XG^T X||_F over G in the subdifferential is 1/2. This invalidates the advertised stationarity equivalence.

The strong-convergence proof contains independent substantive errors. Equation (56) replaces the newly sampled block with the previous block despite the updated iterate depending on that previous selection. Lemma 6.6(b) also incorrectly replaces a root-mean-square bound by a mean bound: with n=3, r=1, k=2, h=0, f(X)=X_2, and X=e_1, its inequality becomes 1 <= sqrt(2/3). Consequently, Theorem 6.8 and the associated convergence rates are not established.

The subproblem solvers do not support their stated guarantees as written. The tangent substitution excludes cos(theta)=0 without evaluating those candidates, and discarding coordinates with y_i=0 is invalid for the l1 penalty because their normalized contributions still depend on t. Section 7.2 also omits the proximal term required by the OBCD-Approx subproblem in Algorithm 1.

Timing comparisons do not adequately isolate algorithmic improvements. Only the proposed breakpoint routine receives a C++ implementation, and warm-start variants receive ten additional seconds without matched baseline-continuation controls. Repeated-run variability and detailed baseline tuning are not reported.

The experimental specification contains a consequential inconsistency: the nonnegative initialization uses 1/|G_i| rather than 1/sqrt(|G_i|), producing non-unit column norms. Since the updates preserve the Gram matrix, this initialization cannot yield the reported orthogonality accuracy. The actual implementation needs clarification, alongside preprocessing, random seeds, and a concrete reproducible code release.

Evidence for scalability and the value of individual components is limited: only k=2 is evaluated, feature dimensions remain at approximately 1,000 or below, and there are no controlled ablations isolating reflections or the specialized subproblem solvers. Direct comparisons with the closest Givens-based coordinate methods are also missing.

strengths: The row-block update preserves orthogonality and provides a practical framework for handling row-separable penalties on rectangular Stiefel matrices.
Reducing two-row updates to scalar problems and considering both rotations and reflections are useful algorithmic design choices.

Experiments cover four problem classes, ten datasets, and multiple ranks and regularization strengths. Several settings show substantial objective improvements, and the nonnegative PCA results demonstrate excellent feasibility preservation.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy in Theorem 5.5 is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix B.8 incorrectly infers a common subgradient from separately satisfiable block conditions. A counterexample uses s=1/sqrt(2), X=[[1,0],[0,s],[0,s]], f(Y)=1.5(Y21-Y31), and h(Y)=||Y||1. With k=2, theta=2, and H=Q=0, X is an exact BS2 point. However, the feasible curve X(t)=[[cos(t),0],[-s*sin(t),s],[s*sin(t),s]] has objective right derivative -s at zero. Thus an exact block-stationary point can have a feasible descent direction, contradicting the claimed stronger-than-critical optimality.

The strong convergence proof contains additional essential gaps. In Appendix B.10, equation (56) replaces the previously selected block with a fresh random block at X^(t+1), although this iterate depends on the previous block. Appendix B.11 converts a root-mean-square residual bound into a mean-residual bound without justification. Appendix B.13 applies the local KL inequality around a global minimizer without establishing that the iterates approach that neighborhood or objective value. Consequently, Theorem 6.8 is not established.

The breakpoint solver is not globally exact as specified. The substitution t=tan(theta) omits cos(theta)=0; even minimizing -sin(theta) has no finite minimizing t. Discarding coordinates with y_i=0 is invalid for the l1 penalty because |x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) remains variable. The printed zero-crossing candidates also use x_i/y_i instead of -x_i/y_i. These issues directly affect the exact-subproblem premise of OBCD-Exact.

The theoretical coverage is narrower than the highlighted applications. Assumption 6.1 requires uniformly bounded subgradients, which fails for the l0 penalty at zeros and the nonnegativity indicator at boundary points. The KL convergence analysis therefore does not cover these principal nonsmooth applications.

The timing evidence does not adequately isolate algorithmic improvements: only OBCD's breakpoint kernel uses C++, while competing methods use MATLAB. Warm-start improvements receive an additional ten seconds without corresponding baseline-continuation controls, so these results do not establish escape from converged critical points. Repeated-run variability, baseline tuning, inner-solver tolerances, and a precise reproducible code release are insufficiently documented.

Important comparisons and ablations are missing, including the closest cited Givens coordinate-descent methods, specialized nonnegative orthogonality solvers, and a rotation-only ablation. All experiments use k=2 and n<=1000, limiting evidence for broader scalability. Performance is also heterogeneous: some baselines substantially outperform OBCD, and Tables 10–11 report very large remaining gradient residuals despite favorable relative objective values.

Reducing two-row updates to scalar optimization over rotations and reflections is a useful algorithmic idea.

strengths: The row-block update preserves orthogonality exactly and applies to rectangular Stiefel matrices. This is a useful framework for optimizing nonsmooth objectives while maintaining feasibility.

For k=2, considering both rotations and reflections reduces the subproblem to one angular variable while covering both components of O(2). The working-set strategies provide practical alternatives to uniform sampling.

The experiments cover four optimization tasks, ten datasets, multiple ranks and regularization levels, and relevant baselines including ManPG and OptM. Several configurations show substantial objective improvements.
weaknesses: The central stationarity equivalence in Theorem 5.5(c) is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix B.8 incorrectly exchanges 'for every block there exists a subgradient' with 'there exists one subgradient for every block.' A counterexample uses a=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,1],[a,0],[a,0]], h(Y) equal to the entrywise l1 norm, and f(Y)=<A,Y>, where A=[[0,-1],[-1,1+a],[-1,-1-a]]. Every two-row subproblem is critical at the identity, but min over G in ∂F(X) of ||G-XGᵀX||_F equals 1. Thus an approximate block-2 stationary point need not be a critical point, invalidating a central theoretical claim.

The strong-convergence proof has independent substantive errors. Lemma 6.6(b) fails even for the smooth example n=r=3, k=2, X=I, h=0, and f(Y)=Y12: its left side is sqrt(2), whereas its right side is sqrt(2/3). Appendix B.11 incorrectly passes from a second-moment bound to the stated first-moment bound. Appendix B.10 also exchanges the previous and next sampled blocks despite the new iterate depending on the previous block. Consequently, the supplied argument does not establish Theorem 6.8.

The claimed exact subproblem solver is incorrect as specified. The substitution t=tan(theta) omits cos(theta)=0; for example, an objective sin(theta) attains its minimum only at an omitted point. The stated zeros of x_i+t*y_i have the wrong sign, and deleting terms with y_i=0 can change the l1 objective because its denominator still depends on t. Section 7.2 also omits the proximal term required by the OBCD-Approx subproblem. These discrepancies matter because the convergence guarantees depend on the subproblem solution properties.

The theoretical coverage is narrower than the broad claims suggest. Uniformly bounded subgradients in Assumption 6.1 exclude the full subdifferentials of l0 penalties at zero and nonnegativity indicators at boundary points. The convergence arguments use uniform random sampling and do not establish the same guarantees for the sampled greedy variants used experimentally.

The empirical evidence does not adequately isolate the algorithmic advantages. Only OBCD's breakpoint solver receives a C++ implementation, complicating interpretation of timing comparisons. There are no repeated-run uncertainty estimates, detailed baseline tuning protocols, or controlled ablations of reflections and the fifth-order solver. Warm-start improvements receive additional computation without a corresponding baseline-continuation control. Tests with n at most 1000 also provide limited evidence for the scalability claim.

There is a consequential reproducibility inconsistency: the nonnegative initialization in Section 9.1 assigns 1/|G_i| within each group, giving squared column norm 1/|G_i| rather than 1. The proposed updates preserve this Gram matrix, so this initialization cannot produce the reported orthogonality accuracy without an undocumented correction. Code availability is described only as 'some Matlab code' on the author's webpages, and exact sampling seeds and reproduction scripts are unspecified.

strengths: The row-block orthogonal update preserves feasibility exactly and provides a useful framework for combining smooth losses with separable nonsmooth penalties.
Reducing two-row updates to one-dimensional rotation/reflection problems is a practical algorithmic contribution.

Experiments cover four problem families, ten datasets, and multiple ranks and regularization settings. They include relevant baselines such as ManPG and OptM and report substantial objective improvements in several settings.
weaknesses: The central stationary-point hierarchy has a fundamental flaw. In Appendix B.8, equations (42)–(44) interchange 'for every block there exists a subgradient' with 'there exists one subgradient satisfying every block.' Overlapping blocks can require incompatible subgradient selections, even with an l1 penalty. Row-wise separability does not resolve this issue, undermining Theorem 5.5(c) and the advertised stronger-than-critical stationarity guarantee.

The strong-convergence proof contains incorrect probabilistic arguments. Equation (56) replaces B^t with B^{t+1} inside an expression involving X^{t+1}, although X^{t+1} depends on B^t. Moreover, Lemma 6.6(b) is false even for a smooth linear objective: with n=3, r=1, k=2, X=e1, and f(X)=X2, its left side equals 1 while its right side equals sqrt(2/3). These errors invalidate the presented justification for Theorem 6.8 and the subsequent convergence-rate claims.

The globally exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Section 7.1 omits cos(theta)=0 when substituting t=tan(theta), although an optimum can occur there. It also incorrectly discards coordinates with y_i=0: their l1 contribution, |x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2), generally depends on t. The stated zero-crossing candidates x_i/y_i should be -x_i/y_i. These problems directly affect the exactness required by OBCD-Exact.

The theoretical coverage is substantially narrower than the application claims suggest. Assumption 6.1 requires bounded subgradients, which fails for the l0 penalty and nonnegativity indicator at zero entries. Consequently, the KL analysis does not cover two prominent nonsmooth applications without additional restrictions.

strengths: The problem is relevant to sparse PCA, nonnegative PCA, and other learning applications. Extending row-based orthogonal updates to rectangular Stiefel matrices is a useful algorithmic direction.

The update preserves XᵀX exactly, and the proximal majorization construction provides a valid sufficient-decrease argument when its subproblem is solved as specified. Considering both rotations and reflections is well motivated.

Experiments cover four problem families, ten data sources, multiple ranks, and regularization strengths. They report substantial objective improvements in several settings and include relevant comparisons with ManPG and OptM.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy in Theorem 5.5 is false under the stated assumptions. Consider n=r=3, k=2, f(X)=X_13, and h(X)=sum_i |sum_j X_ij−1|. This h is convex and row-wise separable. At X=I_3 with Q=0, every exact two-row subproblem is minimized at the identity, including its proximal penalty. Nevertheless, full criticality is impossible: subgradients have entries G_ij=1_{i=1,j=3}+t_i, with t_i in [−1,1], and symmetry requires simultaneously t_1=t_2=t_3 and t_3−t_1=1. Appendix B.8 incorrectly replaces the existence of a subgradient for each block with the existence of one subgradient satisfying every block. Thus exact OBCD can remain at a noncritical point.

The strong-convergence argument contains additional substantive errors. Equation (56) exchanges B^t and B^{t+1} despite X^{t+1} depending on B^t; identical marginal sampling distributions do not justify this equality. Lemma 6.6(b) also fails even for a smooth linear objective: with n=r=3, k=2, X=I_3, h=0, and f(X)=X_12, its claimed inequality becomes sqrt(2) ≤ sqrt(2/3). The proof confuses an expected norm with a root mean square. These errors invalidate the supporting argument for Theorem 6.8.

The breakpoint solver in Section 7.1 is not globally exact as written. The substitution t=tan(theta) omits cos(theta)=0. Zero crossings of x_i+t y_i occur at −x_i/y_i, whereas the stated candidate lists use +x_i/y_i. Furthermore, discarding coordinates with y_i=0 is incorrect for the l1 penalty because their contribution, lambda|x_i|/sqrt(1+t²), still depends on t. These issues directly affect the exact-subproblem requirement.

The theoretical coverage does not match several advertised applications and implementation details. Assumption 6.1 requires bounded subgradients, which excludes the full limiting subdifferentials of the l0 penalty and nonnegativity indicator at zero entries. Section 7.2 also drops the proximal term from Equation (11), so its fifth-order solver does not directly satisfy the analyzed OBCD-Approx specification.

Runtime comparisons need stronger controls. Only the proposed breakpoint solver receives a C++ implementation, while baselines use MATLAB. Baseline tuning, stopping tolerances, repeated-run statistics, and random seeds are insufficiently documented. The experiments also omit direct comparisons with the closest Givens-coordinate methods and ablations isolating reflections and the proposed subproblem solvers.

The empirical superiority claims require qualification. For example, Table 6 on randn with lambda=1 and r=100 reports an objective gap of approximately 1.04e4 for OBCD-OR versus 3.45e−3 for ManPG. Table 11 includes extremely large residuals even for objective-winning OBCD solutions. Fixed-budget improvements relative to the best observed objective do not establish convergence to better stationary solutions.

The experimental specification contains a material feasibility inconsistency. Section 9.1 initializes nonnegative columns using 1/|G_i|, giving squared column norms 1/|G_i| rather than 1; the required normalization is 1/sqrt(|G_i|). Since OBCD preserves the initial Gram matrix, the written procedure cannot produce the reported near-machine-precision feasibility. The initialization and executable implementation need clarification; the vague reference to code on research webpages is insufficient.

strengths: The paper addresses an important optimization class. Orthogonal transformations of selected rows correctly preserve X^T X and provide a useful mechanism for feasible updates on rectangular Stiefel manifolds.
Reducing two-row updates to scalar rotation and reflection subproblems is practically appealing. The sampled greedy working-set strategies also offer a reasonable way to limit selection costs.

The experiments cover four problem families, ten datasets, multiple ranks, and several regularization settings. They report substantial objective improvements in many configurations and include relevant established comparators such as ManPG and OptM.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix B.8 implicitly exchanges 'for every block, there exists a subgradient' with 'there exists one subgradient satisfying every block.' Consider n=r=3, k=2, X=I3, f(X)=<A,X>, A=0.5*[[0,1,-1],[-1,0,1],[1,-1,0]], and h(X)=sum_i |sum_j X_ij-1|. This penalty is convex, Lipschitz, semialgebraic, and row-separable. With Q=0 and any positive proximal parameter, every exact two-row subproblem is globally minimized at I2. Nevertheless, X(t)=exp(-tA) satisfies h(X(t))=0 and has objective derivative -3/2 at t=0; no subgradient at I3 satisfies the full criticality condition. Thus OBCD-Exact can remain at a noncritical point, contradicting Theorem 5.5's claimed implications.

The strong-convergence analysis has independent mathematical errors. Equation (56), step 2, exchanges B^t and B^{t+1} inside an expectation despite X^{t+1} depending on B^t. Lemma 6.6(b) incorrectly converts a root-mean-square bound into a mean bound: even for h=0, f(X)=X_12, X=I3, and k=2, its stated inequality becomes sqrt(2) <= sqrt(2/3). These errors undermine Theorem 6.8. The subsequent rates also refer to a globally optimal solution, although the KL property does not establish global optimality.

The advertised globally exact breakpoint solver is incorrect as written. The substitution t=tan(theta) omits cos(theta)=0, where a global minimizer can occur. Removing coordinates with y_i=0 is also invalid for the l1 case: their contribution lambda*|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) is not constant. Additionally, zeros of x_i+t*y_i occur at -x_i/y_i, whereas the l0 candidate set repeatedly uses the opposite sign. These issues directly affect the exact-subproblem premise of the algorithm.

The runtime comparisons do not adequately isolate algorithmic advantages. Only the proposed breakpoint routine receives a C++ implementation, and the baseline-plus-OBCD experiments add ten seconds without comparing against continued baseline optimization for the same total budget. Baseline tuning, repeated-run variability, and sensitivity to initialization are insufficiently documented.

Important comparisons and ablations are missing, including the cited Givens-coordinate methods and specialized nonnegative-orthogonality solvers. There are no convincing ablations of reflections, block size, or the proximal parameter. Moreover, the large gradient residuals in Tables 10–11 mean that small gaps to the best observed objective do not establish convergence; normalized residuals and comparisons at a common accuracy target are needed.

Reproducibility contains concrete inconsistencies. The nonnegative initialization X^0(G_i,i)=1/|G_i| gives squared column norms 1/|G_i|, rather than one. Since the proposed updates preserve the Gram matrix, this initialization cannot produce the reported orthogonality accuracy without an omitted normalization step. strengths: The row-block update preserves orthogonality exactly and provides a useful foundation for feasible optimization. The sufficient-decrease argument is sound when the specified subproblems are solved as required.
Reducing two-row updates to an angular optimization problem, exploiting structured curvature matrices, and sampling candidate pairs are practical algorithmic ideas.
The experiments cover four optimization tasks, ten data sources, and multiple ranks and regularization parameters. Reported objective improvements and feasibility results are encouraging.
weaknesses: Theorem 5.5(c) is false under the stated row-separability assumption. Its proof incorrectly converts the existence of a suitable subgradient for each block into the existence of one subgradient satisfying every block simultaneously. A counterexample is n=r=3, k=2, f=0, h(X)=sum_i max(X_{i2},X_{i3}), Q=0, theta=2, and X=I_3. Identity minimizes every block surrogate, but any G in the subdifferential has first row (0,a,1-a), with a in [0,1], and G_{21}=G_{31}=0. No such G is symmetric, as criticality at I_3 requires. Thus even OBCD-Exact can stall at a noncritical point.

The strong-convergence analysis contains additional substantive errors. Lemma 6.6(b) effectively replaces sqrt(E[Z^2]) with E[Z], which is not a valid upper bound. For n=3, r=1, k=2, X=e_1, f(X)=X_2, and h=0, its left side equals 1 while its proposed upper bound is sqrt(2/3). Equation (56), step ②, also exchanges B^t and B^{t+1} at X^{t+1}, although X^{t+1} depends on B^t. Their uniform marginal distributions do not justify this exchange. Consequently, Theorem 6.8 lacks a valid proof.

The breakpoint solver does not establish its claimed global exactness. The substitution t=tan(theta) omits cos(theta)=0, which can contain the global minimizer; for example, q(theta)=-2 sin(theta) has no finite minimizing t. Zero crossings are also listed as x_i/y_i rather than -x_i/y_i. Furthermore, discarding coordinates with y_i=0 is invalid for the L1 penalty because |x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) still depends on t. These issues affect candidate construction and the assumptions supporting OBCD-Exact.

The convergence assumptions do not cover several prominently advertised applications. Assumption 6.1 requires bounded nonsmooth subgradients, whereas the L0 penalty at zero and the nonnegativity indicator at boundary points have unbounded subdifferentials. The manuscript needs to delimit its guarantees accordingly or supply different arguments. The fifth-order solver is also developed only for the smooth case h=0.

The experiments do not substantiate the explanation that improvements arise from stronger stationarity. Refining baseline outputs with OBCD for an additional ten seconds requires a control that continues each baseline for the same additional budget. Tables 10–11 also report very large gradient residuals, so their relative objective gaps do not establish convergence to stationary solutions.

Reproducibility and efficiency comparisons need stronger support. Random subsampling and working-set selection are not accompanied by repeated-run statistics, baseline tuning details are insufficient, and code availability is described only through a vague reference to author webpages. Only the proposed breakpoint procedure receives a C++ implementation, complicating attribution of runtime gains. Experiments use n at most 1000 and k=2 throughout, leaving the broader scalability and block-size claims insufficiently tested.

strengths: OBCD addresses a relevant optimization problem. Its row-block orthogonal updates preserve feasibility, and the majorization construction provides a useful descent mechanism when the subproblems are solved as required.
Reducing two-row updates to rotations and reflections is practically appealing. Considering both components of the orthogonal group avoids a real limitation of rotation-only updates.
The experiments cover four problem families and ten datasets, include relevant baselines and working-set comparisons, and report promising objective reductions.
weaknesses: The central stationarity equivalence in Theorem 5.5(c) is false under the stated assumptions. Equation (42) allows a different subgradient for each block, whereas (44) requires one common subgradient. A counterexample uses u=1/√2, X=[[u,0],[1/2,u],[1/2,-u]], h(Y)=||Y||_1, and f(Y)=<A,Y>, where A=[[-1,0],[-1,-1],[-3/2,1+u/2]]. Subgradients at X differ only in G_12=s∈[-1,1]. Stationarity of blocks {1,2} and {1,3} requires s=0 and s=1/2 respectively; block {2,3} is stationary. Thus X is approximately block-2 stationary but is not critical, contradicting a central claimed contribution.

The strong-convergence proof contains substantive errors. Lemma 6.6(b) fails even for a smooth linear objective: with n=r=3, k=2, X=I, and gradient e_1 e_2^T, its left side is √2 while its right side is √(2/3). The proof incorrectly replaces a root-mean-square quantity with a mean. Furthermore, Equation (56) exchanges B^t and B^(t+1) despite X^(t+1) depending on B^t. Consequently, Theorem 6.8 and the associated rates are not established.

The claimed globally exact breakpoint solver is incorrect as written. Lemma 7.1 omits cos(θ)=0; for example, minimizing -sin(θ) becomes a problem whose infimum occurs only at infinite t. Section 7.1 also gives x_i/y_i instead of -x_i/y_i for zero-crossing breakpoints. Its instruction to discard coordinates with y_i=0 is invalid for the ℓ1 case, where λ|x_i|/√(1+t²) still depends on t. These problems undermine the exact-subproblem premise used by the theory.

The advertised generality exceeds the established coverage. The practical breakpoint derivations require coordinate separability, the fifth-order solver is developed only for h=0, and Assumption 6.1's uniform subgradient bound does not hold for the ℓ0 penalty at zero or the nonnegativity indicator at its boundary. Section 7.2 also omits the proximal term required by Equation (11), leaving the connection to the approximate algorithm's decrease guarantee unclear.

The empirical evidence does not adequately isolate algorithmic advantages. OBCD's inner solver uses C++ while the comparisons use MATLAB, baseline tuning and stopping tolerances are insufficiently documented, and repeated-run uncertainty is absent despite randomized sampling. Additional OBCD refinement time does not itself establish stronger stationarity. Tests use k=2 and n≤1000, limiting support for broader scalability claims.

Several specification errors impede reproduction: the nonnegative initializer uses 1/|G_i| instead of 1/√|G_i| and therefore is not orthonormal as stated; the nonlinear eigenvalue objective and gradient use inconsistent A/C notation; and Table 11 labels λ=10000 while its entries specify λ=1000. These require correction alongside the central theoretical issues.

strengths: The row-update scheme preserves orthogonality and avoids full-matrix retractions. The majorization argument provides sufficient decrease when subproblems are solved exactly.
The rotation/reflection parameterization offers a useful way to reduce two-row nonsmooth subproblems to one-dimensional optimization.

Experiments cover ten real or synthetic datasets, three PCA formulations, multiple ranks and regularization strengths, and working-set variants. The appendix includes relevant ManPG comparisons and reports substantial objective improvements on several instances.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix F.2 changes 'for every block there exists a subgradient' into the existence of one subgradient satisfying every block. A counterexample to Theorem 3.6(a) is F(Y)=<A,Y>+||Y||1 on St(3,3), with X=[[0,0.6,0.8],[0.6,0.64,-0.48],[-0.8,0.48,-0.36]] and A=[[-0.03,-0.832,-1.126],[-1,-1.09,0.88],[1,-1.09,0.88]]. Every two-row orthogonal change has F(Y)>=F(X), so X is BS2 with Q=0 and any positive alpha. However, global stationarity requires the subgradient at X11=0 to equal both -0.5 and 0.375. Thus a BS2 point need not even be critical, undermining a principal contribution.

The KL convergence proof contains substantive expectation errors. Equation (48), step 2, exchanges the updated block with a fresh random block even though X^(t+1) depends on the updated block. Equation (54) replaces a root-mean-square quantity with an expected norm; Equation (53) does not justify this. The claimed bound already fails for X=I, k=2, and a smooth linear objective whose skew gradient is supported on one coordinate pair. Theorem 4.8 is therefore unsupported by the supplied proof.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Section 5 places zeros of x_i+t*y_i at +x_i/y_i instead of -x_i/y_i. Its instruction to discard coordinates with y_i=0 is also invalid for the l1 case: such a coordinate contributes lambda*|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2), which affects the minimizer. These errors need correction and solver validation because the algorithmic guarantees assume global subproblem solutions.

The cyclic complexity argument in Theorem 4.2(c) is incomplete. Equation (42) bounds updates evaluated at different iterates across a cycle, then treats that bound as an all-block stationarity certificate at the single final iterate. No stability argument connects these quantities, particularly for nonsmooth objectives.

The nonnegative-PCA initialization in Appendix J.2 uses entries 1/|G_i|, giving squared column norms 1/|G_i| rather than one. Orthogonality requires 1/sqrt(|G_i|). Since OBCD preserves the initial Gram matrix, this description is incompatible with the reported near-machine-precision feasibility unless an unreported normalization was performed.

The empirical evidence does not establish the breadth of the performance claims. Randomized runs lack reported variability and sufficiently documented baseline tuning; warm-start refinements receive additional time without corresponding baseline-continuation controls. Short objective plateaus cannot establish that competitors remain trapped indefinitely. All applications are PCA variants with at most 1,000 optimization rows, limiting evidence for generality and large-scale efficiency.

strengths: The row-wise orthogonal updates preserve feasibility and permit partial-gradient computation. With exact subproblem solutions, the majorization construction provides a useful sufficient-decrease guarantee.
Reducing two-row updates to rotations, reflections, and scalar optimization is a promising approach for handling sparsity penalties.

The experiments cover ten real or synthetic datasets, multiple ranks and regularization strengths, working-set variants, and comparisons including ManPG. Substantial objective improvements are reported on many instances.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy, Theorem 3.6(a), is false under the stated assumptions. Equation (31) allows a different subgradient for each block, whereas the proof requires one common subgradient. A counterexample uses s=1/sqrt(2), X=[[s,0],[1/2,s],[1/2,-s]], f(Y)=<A,Y> with A=[[-1-s,0],[-1,-1],[-1,1]], and h(Y)=||Y||_1. With Q=0, X is block-2 stationary for every alpha>0, yet min_{G in ∂F(X)}||G-XG^T X||_F=1/2. Blocks {1,2} and {1,3} require incompatible choices of the subgradient at X_12. Thus the claimed stronger-than-critical optimality fails even with convex l1 regularization.

The KL convergence proof contains independent substantive errors. Equation (48), step 2, exchanges the previously selected block with a fresh random block despite X^{t+1} depending on the former. Equations (53)–(54) also incorrectly replace a root-mean-square quantity with its mean. For n=3, r=1, k=2, h=0, f(x)=x_2, and X=e_1, the claimed bound in (54) would require 1<=sqrt(2/3). Consequently, Theorem 4.8 is not established.

The cyclic complexity argument in Theorem 4.2(c) bounds steps evaluated at different iterates within a cycle. Equation (42) does not establish the all-block stationarity residual at the cycle endpoint required by Definition 4.1.

The exact breakpoint solver is incorrect as written. Solving x_i+t*y_i=0 requires t=-x_i/y_i, but Section 5 lists the positive ratio. Moreover, discarding coordinates with y_i=0 changes the l1 objective because |x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) is not constant. These errors undermine the exact-subproblem assumption used throughout the analysis.

The nonnegative PCA initialization in Appendix J.2 assigns 1/|G_i| rather than 1/sqrt(|G_i|), producing columns with squared norm 1/|G_i|. Since OBCD preserves the initial Gram matrix, this stated protocol cannot produce Table 5's near-machine-precision feasibility without an unreported normalization.

Experimental support remains incomplete: there are no repeated-run uncertainty estimates, insufficient baseline-tuning details, and no substantive sensitivity studies for alpha or the majorizer. All experiments use k=2 and quadratic PCA objectives, leaving the broader algorithmic scope unvalidated. The reported empirical gains do not resolve the fundamental failures in the central theoretical claims.

strengths: Addresses a relevant optimization problem with simple row updates that preserve orthogonality and can avoid expensive full-matrix retractions.
The k=2 reduction to one-dimensional problems, including both rotations and reflections, offers a useful algorithmic approach to nonsmooth objectives.

Experiments cover ten datasets, three PCA formulations, multiple ranks and regularization strengths, and working-set variants. The appendix includes relevant ManPG comparisons and reports substantial objective improvements on several instances.
weaknesses: The central optimality claim, Theorem 3.6(a), is false under the stated assumptions. Equation (31) incorrectly assumes that subgradients satisfying individual block conditions can be chosen consistently across all blocks. A counterexample uses u=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,u,u],[u,1/2,-1/2],[u,-1/2,1/2]], h(Y)=||Y||₁, and f(Y)=<A,Y>, where A=[[0,-1-u/2,-1+u/2],[-1,-1,1],[-1,1,-1]]. Each two-row block admits a subgradient G with [GXᵀ]BB=0, so X is block-2 stationary for Q=0 and any α>0. However, full criticality requires the subgradient at X₁₁=0 to equal both 1/2 and -1/2. This directly contradicts the advertised hierarchy.

The KL convergence proof contains substantive errors. Equation (48), step ②, exchanges the previous and newly sampled blocks even though Xᵗ⁺¹ depends on the previous block. Additionally, Equation (53) gives a root-mean-square identity, whereas Equation (54) incorrectly replaces the root mean square by the mean. These steps do not establish Lemma 4.7 or the finite-length claim in Theorem 4.8.

The cyclic iteration bound in Theorem 4.2(c) is unsupported. Equation (42) bounds updates evaluated at different iterates throughout a cycle, then treats that bound as an ε-block-stationarity certificate at the cycle endpoint. No argument connects these different evaluation points.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as specified. Section 5 and Appendix B list t=xᵢ/yᵢ as a zero-crossing breakpoint, although xᵢ+tyᵢ=0 requires t=-xᵢ/yᵢ. Discarding coordinates with yᵢ=0 is also invalid for ℓ₁ regularization because their contribution |xᵢ|/sqrt(1+t²) depends on t. These errors undermine the exact-solve guarantee on which the analysis relies.

The nonnegative-PCA initialization in Appendix J.2 uses X⁰(Gᵢ,i)=1/|Gᵢ|, producing squared column norms 1/|Gᵢ| rather than one. Since OBCD preserves the initial Gram matrix, this initialization cannot produce the near-machine-precision feasibility reported in Table 5. The formula should use 1/sqrt(|Gᵢ|), and the actual implementation needs clarification.

The empirical evidence lacks repeated-run uncertainty, sufficient baseline tuning and preprocessing details, and convergence diagnostics supporting the claimed escape from inferior stationary points. Warm-start experiments give OBCD an additional ten seconds without matched baseline-continuation controls. Short runtime plots cannot justify Figure 1's assertion that competing methods remain trapped regardless of runtime. These limitations compound the fundamental theoretical problems.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant optimization class encompassing sparse PCA and nonnegative PCA, including discontinuous regularizers.

The orthogonal row-block update preserves feasibility, and the majorization argument supports sufficient decrease when subproblems are solved globally. Using partial gradients and small subproblems is computationally attractive.

The experiments report substantial objective improvements: OBCD-R achieves the best reported objective in 35 of 40 settings in Table 1. The appendix includes working-set comparisons, different ranks and regularization strengths, and ManPG comparisons for ℓ1 regularization.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy has a substantive proof gap. In Appendix F.2, block optimality supplies a potentially different subgradient G_B for each block in Equation (31), but Equation (32) assumes one subgradient simultaneously satisfies every block condition. This exchanges 'for every block there exists a subgradient' with 'there exists a subgradient for every block.' Overlapping row rotations couple these choices; ambient coordinate separability does not justify the exchange. Consequently, the claimed implication from block stationarity to criticality is not established.

The KL convergence proof contains invalid probabilistic arguments. Equation (48) substitutes the previously selected block for a fresh random block even though the updated iterate depends on the previous selection. Equation (54) also replaces a root-mean-square quantity with a mean, which Equation (53) does not permit. For n=r=3, k=2, X=I, h=0, and f(X)=X_12, the claimed bound requires sqrt(2) ≤ sqrt(2/3). These errors undermine Theorem 4.8.

The cyclic complexity guarantee in Theorem 4.2(c) is unsupported. Equation (42) bounds update magnitudes evaluated at different iterates throughout a cycle, then identifies this with the all-block stationarity measure at the cycle's final iterate. No argument controls the changes in the other block subproblems between those iterates.

The stated exact breakpoint solver contains consequential errors. Section 5 gives t=x_i/y_i for zeros of x_i+t y_i; the correct sign is negative. It also discards coordinates with y_i=0, although their ℓ1 contribution is |x_i|/sqrt(1+t²), which can change the minimizer. The global subproblem optimality guarantee needs corrected formulas and verification.

The nonnegative initialization in Appendix J.2 is inconsistent with the reported feasibility. Setting X(G_i,i)=1/|G_i| gives column squared norm 1/|G_i|, rather than 1. Since OBCD preserves the Gram matrix, this initialization cannot yield the near-machine-precision orthogonality reported in Table 5. The actual implementation requires clarification.

The empirical conclusions exceed the available controls. Randomized experiments lack reported variability and sufficiently detailed baseline tuning; warm-start improvements receive an additional ten seconds without matched baseline-continuation controls. Short objective traces cannot establish the claim that competing methods remain trapped regardless of runtime. Experiments also omit a rotation-only ablation and evaluate only k=2, limiting evidence for the broader algorithmic claims.

strengths: The row-wise orthogonal update is a useful construction: it preserves feasibility, supports rectangular Stiefel matrices, and permits partial-gradient computations.
Reducing the k=2 subproblem to one-dimensional searches over rotations and reflections is a promising practical approach to nonsmooth constrained optimization.

The experiments cover ten datasets, three PCA formulations, multiple ranks and regularization strengths, and working-set variants. The appendix includes relevant comparisons with ManPG and reports substantial objective improvements in many settings.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy in Theorem 3.6(a) is false under the stated assumptions. Equation (31) permits a different subgradient G for each block, whereas the proof subsequently assumes one G works for every block. A counterexample is q=1/√2, X=[[0,q],[q,1/2],[q,-1/2]], f(Y)=-Y21-Y22-Y31+Y32, h(Y)=||Y||1, H=Q=0, and α=1. Here I2 globally minimizes every two-row surrogate, so X is a BS2-point. However, ∂F(X) consists of G=[[s,1],[0,0],[0,0]] with |s|≤1, and the minimum of ||G-XGᵀX||F is q>0. Thus X is not critical, directly contradicting the paper's principal stronger-optimality claim.

The KL convergence proof contains additional substantive errors. Equation (48), step ②, exchanges the previously selected block with a fresh random block even though X^(t+1) depends on the previous selection. Equations (53)–(54) also replace a root-mean-square quantity with a mean without justification. Indeed, for h=0, f(x)=-x2 on St(3,1), x=e1, and k=2, the claimed bound in (54) becomes 1≤√(2/3), which is false. Consequently, the finite-length guarantee in Theorem 4.8 is not established.

The cyclic complexity guarantee in Theorem 4.2(c) is unsupported. Equation (42) bounds an average of updates evaluated at different iterates within a cycle, then declares the cycle endpoint approximately stationary for every block. No argument transfers these individual update bounds to the common point required by Definition 4.1.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Section 5 and Appendix B use t=xi/yi for a zero of xi+t yi; the correct breakpoint is -xi/yi. Furthermore, removing coordinates with yi=0 is invalid for the ℓ1 case because λ|xi|/√(1+t²) still depends on t. These errors can omit minimizers and undermine the exact-solution assumption supporting the algorithm's guarantees.

The empirical evidence does not establish the claimed explanation of escaping poor local minima through stronger stationarity. No stationarity certificates or repeated-run uncertainty are reported, and baseline tuning details are insufficient. The hybrid experiments give OBCD an additional ten seconds without an equivalent baseline-continuation control. Moreover, all applications share a quadratic PCA smooth term and use k=2, leaving the broader generality and scalability claims weakly tested. The numerical successes do not resolve the fundamental theoretical counterexample.

strengths: The row-block update preserves orthogonality and offers a useful way to exploit partial gradients and incremental computations.
Reducing two-row subproblems to one-dimensional searches over rotations and reflections is a promising computational approach for nonsmooth penalties.

The experiments provide substantial positive evidence: OBCD-R achieves the lowest reported objective in 35 of Table 1’s 40 settings. The appendix broadens coverage to nonnegative PCA and ℓ1-SPCA, including ManPG comparisons and working-set variants.

Equation (31) permits a different subgradient for each block, whereas Lemma A.1 requires one common subgradient. Equation (48) interchanges the previously selected block with a fresh random block, although the updated iterate depends on the previous selection. Equation (54) incorrectly replaces a root-mean-square quantity by a mean norm. These steps undermine the KL finite-length argument. Nonnegative PCA comparisons omit specialized methods already cited in the manuscript. Hybrid methods receive an additional ten seconds without an equivalent continuation control for the baseline. strengths: The paper addresses an important optimization class relevant to sparse and nonnegative PCA.

The row-wise orthogonal update preserves feasibility, and exact minimization of the majorizing subproblem supports the basic sufficient-decrease result. Searching both rotations and reflections covers all of O(2).

The experiments cover ten datasets, three PCA formulations, multiple ranks and regularization weights, working-set strategies, and refinement of baseline solutions. The appendix includes relevant ManPG comparisons and reports substantial objective improvements.
weaknesses: The central optimality hierarchy, Theorem 3.6(a), is false as stated. Equations (31)–(32) replace 'for every block B, there exists a subgradient G_B' with the existence of one subgradient satisfying every block. A concrete counterexample uses c=1/sqrt(2), X0=[[0,c,c],[c,1/2,-1/2],[c,-1/2,1/2]], A=[[0,1/4,-1/4],[-1/4,0,0],[1/4,0,0]], h(Y)=||Y||_1, and f(Y)=<AX0-S,Y>, where S equals sign(X0) except S11=0. Every two-row orthogonal update has F(Y)>=F(X0), making X0 a BS2 point for Q=0 and any alpha>0. Nevertheless, the feasible tangent direction -AX0 has directional derivative -1/4. Thus BS2 points need not be critical, directly contradicting a principal contribution.

The KL convergence proof contains independent substantive gaps. Equation (48), step 2, exchanges the previous and newly sampled blocks even though X^(t+1) depends on the previous block. Equation (54) incorrectly converts an identity involving expected squared norms into one involving expected norms; it also does not justify combining separately minimized block subgradients into a global residual. The error bounds needed for Theorem 4.8 are therefore not established.

The cyclic complexity claim in Theorem 4.2(c) does not follow from Equation (42). Small average update sizes at different iterates within a cycle do not establish the required all-block stationarity measure at the single endpoint iterate. A valid argument transferring these quantities to a common iterate is missing.

The exact breakpoint solver is incorrect as written. Section 5 and Appendix B list x_i/y_i as zeros of x_i+t*y_i, whereas the correct breakpoint is -x_i/y_i. Section 5 also discards coordinates with y_i=0, although for the L1 penalty they contribute lambda*|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2), which can change the minimizer. These issues require correction and verification against the implementation.

The nonnegative PCA initialization in Appendix J.2 assigns entries 1/|G_i|, giving column squared norms 1/|G_i| rather than 1. Because OBCD preserves the initial Gram matrix, this initialization cannot yield the reported orthogonality residuals. The manuscript must clarify whether 1/sqrt(|G_i|) was actually used.

The empirical conclusions exceed the evidence. Randomized sampling and block selection are reported without variability across seeds, baseline tuning and preprocessing are insufficiently specified, and nonnegative PCA comparisons omit the specialized exact-penalty methods already cited. All nonsmooth experiments use k=2. Short objective-versus-time comparisons and additional refinement time do not establish that competing methods are permanently trapped in local minima or attribute improvements to the claimed stationarity hierarchy.

strengths: The row-update construction preserves orthogonality exactly and offers inexpensive iterations. The sufficient-descent argument is sound under exact surrogate minimization.
Reducing two-row updates to optimization over rotations and reflections is a useful approach to handling nonsmooth penalties while maintaining feasibility.
The experiments cover ten datasets and three PCA formulations, with several relevant baselines, runtime curves, and substantial supplementary detail.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy has a substantive flaw. In Theorem 3.8(a), Equation (38) permits a different subgradient G_B for each block, but Lemma A.1 requires one common G satisfying every block condition. Coordinate separability does not resolve this after overlapping row rotations. Even with linear f and an L1 penalty, different blocks can require incompatible values of the same subgradient entry. A sufficiently large proximal term can make each surrogate globally minimized at the identity without establishing criticality. The same invalid interchange of subgradient minimization and block averaging appears in Equation (58).

The convergence guarantees have additional serious gaps. Equations (51)–(52) exchange expectations over the previous and next sampled blocks despite the evaluated matrix depending on the previous block through X^(t+1). Appendix F.4 then uses expectation bounds as pointwise inequalities and extracts a random objective difference from an expectation. It also substitutes F∞, defined as the global infimum, for the limiting objective value without justification. Consequently, the advertised critical-point complexity and KL convergence rates are not established.

The main L0 experiments reduce to a simple selection problem. Appendix G.2 normalizes A so that tr(C)=1, implying 0≤tr(XᵀCX)≤1. With every tested λ≥10, any solution having more than r nonzeros is worse than a solution with exactly r nonzeros. The global optimum therefore consists of signed coordinate vectors selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact baseline is missing, and the experiments do not establish effectiveness in a meaningful sparsity–variance tradeoff regime.

The breakpoint solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B identifies zeros of x_i+t y_i at t=x_i/y_i instead of -x_i/y_i. It also states that entries with y_i=0 can be discarded, although their L1 contribution |x_i|/sqrt(1+t²) remains variable. These issues directly affect the claimed exact subproblem solution and require correction and verification.

Experimental comparisons do not adequately isolate algorithmic benefits. All L1 baselines use random initialization while OBCD uses identity initialization, which already has minimum possible L1 norm. Repeated-run variability, comprehensive baseline tuning, and matched-initialization comparisons are absent. Timing is also inconsistent: the main text specifies 30 seconds, Table 1 specifies 40 seconds, and the curves extend to 60 seconds.

The demonstrated scope is narrower than the general framework suggests. Efficient global subproblem solution is assumed for arbitrary k and h, while constructive treatment primarily covers k=2 and selected penalties. There are no substantive ablations of block size, reflections, surrogate choice, or the proximal parameter to establish which components produce the reported gains.

strengths: The row-wise orthogonal update preserves feasibility exactly, and the majorization argument provides a useful sufficient-decrease property.
Reducing two-row updates to one-dimensional rotation and reflection searches is a promising approach to separable nonsmooth optimization on the Stiefel manifold.
Experiments cover three PCA formulations and ten datasets, including relevant baselines such as ManPG, RADMM, and RSSM.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Consider a=1/sqrt(2), b=1+a/2, X=[(a,0);(a,0);(0,1)], f(Y)=b(Y12-Y22), h(Y)=||Y||1, Q=0, and α=1. Identity globally minimizes every two-row surrogate at X, making X a BS2 point. However, criticality would require the same subgradient entry H31 to satisfy both H31≥1/2 and H31≤-1/2. Indeed, the full stationarity residual in Definition 3.4 is 1/2, while every block residual is zero. This contradicts Theorem 3.8(a) and Lemma 4.4(b), and OBCD initialized here never reaches a critical point. Appendix E.3 incorrectly replaces block-specific subgradient choices with a single common choice.

The stochastic convergence proofs have additional substantive gaps. Equations (51)–(52) interchange the selected block and a fresh block although the iterate X^{t+1} depends on the selected block. The KL proof also uses bounds in expectation inside products with random objective decreases and substitutes the global infimum for the limiting objective value without justification. Consequently, the claimed criticality complexity and KL convergence rates are not established.

The main ℓ0-SPCA benchmark becomes an elementary coordinate-selection problem. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||F=1, implying tr(C)=1 and 0≤tr(XᵀCX)≤1. Every tested λ exceeds 1. Any feasible matrix with at least r+1 nonzeros therefore costs at least λ(r+1)-1>λr, whereas a coordinate basis costs at most λr. The global optimum must have exactly r nonzeros and is obtained by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact baseline is missing, and these parameter settings do not demonstrate performance on nontrivial sparse PCA instances.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B discards coordinates with yi=0, although their ℓ1 contribution |xi|/sqrt(1+t²) still depends on t. It also lists xi/yi as a zero of xi+tyi, which requires -xi/yi. These issues require correction and implementation verification because the main guarantees assume globally solved subproblems.

The remaining empirical evidence does not isolate the algorithmic contribution convincingly. For ℓ1-SPCA and nonnegative PCA, OBCD uses identity initialization while competitors use random initialization. Repeated-run variability, baseline tuning details, and ablations of reflections, surrogate choice, and block size are missing. Matched initializations and meaningful regularization regimes are needed to support the broad superiority claims.

strengths: Addresses an important class of nonsmooth optimization problems. The row-wise orthogonal updates preserve feasibility exactly and permit inexpensive partial-gradient computations.
The majorization construction provides sufficient descent when subproblems are solved correctly. Searching both rotations and reflections offers a practical approach to two-row updates.
Experiments cover ten real or synthetic datasets and three PCA formulations, with relevant baselines, objective-versus-time plots, and nonnegativity residuals.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix E.3 moves from a potentially different subgradient for each block in (38) to one common subgradient in (39). A counterexample is n=3, r=k=2, X=[[a,0],[a,b],[a,-b]], a=1/sqrt(3), b=1/sqrt(2), f(Y)=-Y21-Y22-Y31+Y32, h(Y)=||Y||1, H=Q=0, and alpha=1. The identity globally minimizes every block surrogate, but the paper's squared critical residual min_G ||G-XG^T X||_F^2 equals 2/3. Blocks (1,2) and (1,3) require incompatible subgradient entries G12=-sqrt(2/3) and +sqrt(2/3). Thus Theorem 3.8(a), Lemma 4.4(b), and Theorem 4.6 fail for an admissible convex nonsmooth regularizer.

The randomized convergence proofs contain additional substantive gaps. Equation (52), step 2, replaces the fresh block B^(t+1) with B^t although X^(t+1) depends on B^t. Appendix F.4 then uses expectation bounds as pointwise bounds and removes a random objective-decrease factor from conditional expectation. It also substitutes the global infimum F∞ for the limiting objective value in the KL argument without establishing their equality. These steps do not establish the claimed last-iterate rates.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B lists t=x_i/y_i as a breakpoint for x_i+t*y_i=0, where the correct sign is negative. It also discards coordinates with y_i=0, although their ℓ1 contribution |x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) remains variable. These errors can omit minimizers and undermine the essential exact-solution assumption.

The main ℓ0 benchmarks are degenerate under the stated normalization. Appendix G.2 sets ||A||_F=1, implying trace(C)=1 and 0≤trace(X^T C X)≤1. Every tested lambda is at least 10, so any solution with more than r nonzeros is worse than a coordinate basis with r nonzeros. The global optimum therefore follows simply by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact baseline is missing, and the results do not demonstrate performance on nontrivial sparse PCA tradeoffs.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate algorithmic gains. For ℓ1 PCA and nonnegative PCA, OBCD uses identity initialization while competitors use random initialization. There are no reported multi-seed uncertainty estimates or matched-initialization ablations, and baseline tuning is insufficiently specified. Ablations of reflections, surrogate choice, and the proximal parameter are also missing. The main text states a 30-second budget while Table 1 states 40 seconds.

The demonstrated scope is narrower than the broad claims suggest: constructive nonsmooth global subproblem solvers are provided only for k=2, while general k relies on an oracle assumption. Moreover, the bounded-subgradient assumption required for the stronger convergence results excludes the ℓ0 regularizer and nonnegativity indicator used in two experimental applications.

Extending rotation-based coordinate updates to rectangular Stiefel matrices and nonsmooth penalties is useful. The two-row reduction provides a practical algorithmic direction.

The demonstrated scope is substantially narrower than the broad claims: practical nonsmooth experiments use two-row updates and only PCA variants, with n at most 1000. The row updates preserve orthogonality exactly. The majorization construction and basic sufficient-descent argument provide a useful foundation for inexpensive partial-gradient iterations.
The two-row reduction to rotations and reflections is constructive, and the experiments cover three applications, ten datasets, and several relevant contemporary baselines.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Equations (38)–(39) incorrectly replace a separately chosen subgradient for each block with one common subgradient. A concrete counterexample uses h(Y)=||Y||_1, f(Y)=<A,Y>, A=[[-1,0],[-1/2,-1],[-1/2,1]], X=[[1/√2,0],[1/2,1/√2],[1/2,-1/√2]], k=2, Q=0, and α=1. For every row pair, K(V;X,B)-K(I;X,B)≥||V-I||_F²/4, so X is a global BS2 point and every update stays at X. Nevertheless, min over G∈∂F(X) of ||G-XGᵀX||_F equals 1/2. This directly contradicts Theorem 3.8(a), Lemma 4.4(b), and the critical-point convergence guarantee in Theorem 4.6.

The stochastic and KL proofs contain additional substantive gaps. Equation (52) swaps the previously selected block with a fresh independent block even though X^{t+1} depends on the previous selection. Appendix F.4 subsequently applies expected bounds as pointwise inequalities and removes random factors from expectations without justification. It also substitutes the global infimum F∞ for the limiting objective value when applying the local KL inequality. The claimed last-iterate rates are therefore unsupported.

The main L0-SPCA evaluation is mathematically degenerate. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, implying 0≤tr(XᵀCX)≤1. With every tested λ≥10, any feasible matrix with more than r nonzeros is worse than an r-sparse coordinate frame. Consequently, the global optimum is obtained simply by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This elementary exact baseline is missing, and the experiments do not establish effectiveness on a meaningful sparsity–variance tradeoff.

The breakpoint solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B lists x_i/y_i as the zero of x_i+t y_i, whereas the correct breakpoint is -x_i/y_i. It also permits deleting coordinates with y_i=0, although their L1 contribution |x_i|/√(1+t²) generally depends on t. These errors undermine the described solver's exactness, which the main guarantees require.

The empirical comparisons do not isolate algorithmic advantages adequately. L1-SPCA and nonnegative-PCA baselines use random initialization while OBCD uses identity initialization. Repeated-run statistics, sufficiently detailed baseline tuning, and ablations of reflections, curvature choices, and proximal parameters are absent. The main text also specifies a 30-second budget while Table 1 states 40 seconds.

The practical scope and novelty are narrower than the framing suggests. Tractable nonsmooth subproblem procedures are developed only for k=2; efficient global solution for general k is assumed. Reachability largely follows classical Givens/QR constructions and does not establish that the monotone optimization algorithm can escape arbitrary poor local minima.

strengths: The paper addresses an important optimization setting combining nonsmooth penalties with orthogonality constraints, with clear relevance to sparse representation learning.

The row-wise orthogonal update preserves feasibility exactly. The majorization construction and sufficient-descent argument provide a useful algorithmic foundation, while partial-gradient updates offer potential computational savings.

The rotation/reflection parameterization makes two-row subproblems tractable for several useful penalties. Experiments cover three PCA formulations and ten datasets; Table 3 reports promising nonnegative-PCA objectives with negligible nonnegativity violations.
weaknesses: The central claim that block-2 stationarity implies criticality is false under the stated assumptions. Equations (38)–(39) incorrectly replace a potentially different subgradient for each block with one common subgradient. A counterexample uses n=3, r=k=2, f(Y)=<A,Y>, h(Y)=||Y||_1, Q=0, and α=1, with q=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,q],[q,1/2],[q,-1/2]], and A=[[0,-1],[-1,-3/2],[-1,3/2]]. Every two-row surrogate is globally minimized at I: for each block, an appropriate subgradient makes L_B=G_B X_B^T symmetric with largest eigenvalue at most 1/4, giving K(V)-K(I)≥<V-I,L_B-I>≥0. However, the full subgradients are G(s)=[[s,0],[0,-1/2],[0,1/2]], |s|≤1, and ||G(s)-XG(s)^T X||_F²=3s²/2+1/4. Thus X is block-2 stationary but not critical. This directly contradicts Theorem 3.8(a), Lemma 4.4(b), and the claimed general convergence to critical points.

The convergence analysis contains additional substantive errors. Equation (51) exchanges the updated block B_t with an independent next block even when the matrix being sampled depends on X^{t+1}, hence on B_t. Equal marginal sampling distributions do not justify this exchange. Appendix F.4 also uses expected bounds as pointwise inequalities and removes random objective differences from expectations. Furthermore, the KL argument substitutes the global infimum F∞ for the limiting objective value without establishing their equality. The advertised last-iterate guarantees are therefore unsupported.

The main ℓ0-SPCA benchmarks collapse to an elementary problem. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, so C=A^T A has trace 1 and tr(X^T C X)≤1. With every tested λ≥10, any feasible matrix having more than r nonzeros has objective at least λ(r+1)-1>λr, whereas a coordinate frame has objective at most λr. Consequently, a global optimum consists of the coordinate vectors corresponding to the r largest diagonal entries of C. This sorting baseline is absent, and these experiments do not establish performance on a substantive sparsity–variance tradeoff.

The claimed exact breakpoint solver has errors as written. Appendix B discards coordinates with y_i=0, although their ℓ1 contribution λ|x_i|/sqrt(1+t²) generally depends on t. It also lists ℓ0 zero-crossing candidates as x_i/y_i, whereas x_i+t y_i=0 requires -x_i/y_i. These affect the exact-subproblem assumption on which the guarantees depend and require implementation verification. For general nonsmooth penalties with k>2, efficient global subproblem solution is assumed rather than demonstrated.

The remaining empirical evidence lacks important controls. For ℓ1-SPCA and nonnegative PCA, OBCD uses identity initialization while competitors use random initialization, confounding algorithmic gains with starting-point effects. Repeated-run variability, sufficiently documented baseline tuning, and ablations isolating reflections and surrogate choices are missing. The stated 30-second comparison budget also disagrees with Table 1's 40-second budget. These limitations prevent the promising numerical results from compensating for the fundamental theoretical and evaluation problems.

strengths: Row-wise orthogonal updates preserve feasibility exactly, accommodate rectangular Stiefel matrices, and avoid full retractions.

The majorization construction provides a useful sufficient-decrease property under exact subproblem minimization. Reducing two-row updates to rotation/reflection searches is computationally appealing.
Experiments cover three PCA formulations and ten datasets, with relevant ManPG, RSSM, and ADMM-family comparisons and substantial reported objective improvements.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Consider h(Y)=||Y||₁, f(Y)=−Y₂₁−Y₂₂−Y₃₁+Y₃₂, and X=[[s,0],[1/2,s],[1/2,−s]], where s=1/√2. With Q=0 and α=1, every two-row surrogate is globally minimized at I₂, making X a BS₂ point. Nevertheless, min_{G∈∂F(X)} ||G−XGᵀX||_F²=1/2, so X is not critical. Equation (38) incorrectly assumes that subgradients satisfying individual block conditions can be chosen consistently across all blocks. This invalidates Theorem 3.8(a) and Lemma 4.4(b), undermining the claimed stronger optimality and critical-point convergence.

The stochastic convergence proofs contain additional substantive gaps. Equations (51)–(52) replace a freshly sampled block with the block that generated X^{t+1}, although the residual at X^{t+1} depends on that previous block. Appendix F.4 subsequently uses expectation bounds as pointwise inequalities and factors correlated random quantities. Consequently, the advertised KL-based finite-length and last-iterate rates are not established by the supplied arguments.

The main ℓ0 evaluation uses a degenerate regularization regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, giving tr(C)=1 and −tr(XᵀCX)∈[−1,0], while every tested λ is at least 10. Any solution with more than r nonzeros therefore loses to a coordinate solution. The global optimum is obtained simply by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact sorting baseline is missing, and these benchmarks do not demonstrate performance on nontrivial sparse-PCA tradeoffs.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as described in Appendix B. Terms with y_i=0 are discarded, although for ℓ1 regularization they contribute λ|x_i|/√(1+t²), which affects the minimizer. The listed zeros of x_i+t y_i also have the wrong sign: they should be −x_i/y_i. These errors require correction and verification because exact global subproblem solutions underpin the main guarantees.

Experimental controls do not adequately isolate the algorithmic contribution. For ℓ1 SPCA, OBCD receives identity initialization while every baseline receives random initialization; identity initialization already minimizes the dominant sparsity penalty. Matched initialization, repeated-run uncertainty, and ablations of reflections, block size, and the proximal parameter are missing. Runtime reporting is also inconsistent: the prose specifies 30 seconds, Table 1 specifies 40, and appendix tables specify 60.
