strengths: The row-update construction preserves orthogonality exactly and offers an appealing way to use partial gradients without full-matrix retractions. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260913-01/reviews/review-experiment-gl6x9rsx/call-36a2db15ef2642a09bc3c07d586a4f2c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The majorization construction provides a valid sufficient-descent mechanism under exact subproblem solution. Considering both rotations and reflections gives a useful scalar reduction for two-row updates.
Experiments cover ten datasets and three PCA formulations, with relevant baselines including ManPG, RSSM, and RADMM. The reported nonnegative-PCA results suggest practical promise.
weaknesses: The central stationarity claim, Theorem 3.8(a), is false under the stated assumptions. Consider n=3, r=k=2, q=1/√2, X=[[0,1],[q,0],[q,0]], f(Y)=1.5(Y_22−Y_32), h(Y)=||Y||_1, H=Q=0, and α=1. For every row pair, I_2 globally minimizes K(V;X,B), yet the squared full stationarity residual defined in the paper equals 1/2. Thus OBCD can remain indefinitely at a noncritical BS2 point. Equations (38)–(39) incorrectly replace a potentially different subgradient for each block with one subgradient satisfying every block condition. Coordinate separability does not justify this exchange for overlapping row rotations. This counterexample also invalidates Lemma 4.4(b) and Theorem 4.6.

The stochastic and KL proofs contain additional substantive gaps. Equations (51)–(52) interchange the previous and freshly sampled blocks although X^{t+1} depends on the previous block; identical sampling distributions do not justify that substitution. Appendix F.4 subsequently uses expectation bounds as pointwise inequalities and removes correlated random factors from expectations. It also conflates the global infimum F∞ with the limiting objective required by the KL argument. The claimed finite-length and last-iterate guarantees therefore lack valid support.

The main ℓ0 experiments evaluate an analytically trivial regularization regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, so C=AᵀA has trace 1 and 0≤tr(XᵀCX)≤1. Every feasible X has at least r nonzeros. With every tested λ≥10, any additional nonzero costs more than the entire possible variance improvement. Consequently, a global optimum consists of the coordinate axes corresponding to the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact sorting baseline is absent, and the experiments do not establish performance on nontrivial sparsity–variance tradeoffs.

The breakpoint solver is incorrect as described in Appendix B. Zero crossings satisfy t=−x_i/y_i, whereas the listed candidates use the opposite sign. Discarding coordinates with y_i=0 is also invalid for ℓ1 regularization: their contribution λ|x_i|/√(1+t²) still depends on t. These terms must be retained or incorporated into other coefficients before exactness can be claimed.

Experimental controls are insufficient for the broad superiority claims. The ℓ1 and nonnegative-PCA comparisons use identity initialization for OBCD and random initialization for competitors. Matched-start ablations, repeated-run uncertainty, reflection ablations, and convincing scaling studies are missing, while baseline tuning is insufficiently specified. The main text also states a 30-second budget whereas Table 1 states 40 seconds. These limitations compound the fundamental theoretical and evaluation problems above.

strengths: The problem is relevant to sparse learning and manifold optimization. Updating selected rows through small orthogonal transformations preserves feasibility and avoids full retractions.
The majorization construction provides a useful sufficient-decrease guarantee when the block subproblem is solved correctly.
The two-row reduction to scalar optimization is practically appealing. Experiments cover three PCA variants and ten datasets, with relevant baselines including ManPG, RADMM, and RSSM.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Equation (38) allows a different subgradient for each block, whereas Equation (39) requires one common subgradient. A counterexample uses n=3, r=k=2, Q=0, alpha=1, h(X)=||X||_1, and f(X)=<A,X>, with A=[[-1,0],[-3/2,-1],[3/2,-1]] and X=[[s,0],[1/2,s],[-1/2,s]], s=1/sqrt(2). Every block surrogate is globally minimized at I_2: suitable block subgradients produce symmetric G_B X_B^T with largest eigenvalue at most 1/4. Nevertheless, the full subgradients are G(z)=[[0,z],[-1/2,0],[1/2,0]], |z|<=1, and ||G(z)-XG(z)^T X||_F^2=1/4+3z^2/2. Thus OBCD can remain at a noncritical point, contradicting Theorem 3.8(a), Lemma 4.4(b), and Theorem 4.6.

The convergence proofs contain additional substantive gaps. Equation (51) exchanges the updated block with an independent subsequent block even though X^{t+1} depends on the updated block. Appendix F.4 applies bounds in expectation as pointwise bounds inside products and takes random quantities outside expectations. It also replaces the limiting objective value in the KL inequality with F_infinity, previously defined as the global infimum. Consequently, the claimed last-iterate guarantees are not established.

The main experimental regime makes the intended L0 problem elementary. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, so tr(C)=1 and the total variance reward is at most 1. All tested penalties satisfy lambda>=10; therefore, any solution with more than r nonzeros is worse than a coordinate-basis solution. The global optimum follows by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact sorting baseline is missing, and the experiments do not test a meaningful variance–sparsity tradeoff.

The supposedly exact breakpoint solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B gives x_i/y_i as a root of x_i+t y_i=0 instead of -x_i/y_i. It also says terms with y_i=0 can be discarded, although their L1 contribution |x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) depends on t. These issues require correction and verification because exact block minimization is a foundational assumption.

The empirical comparisons do not adequately isolate the algorithmic advantage. For L1 PCA, OBCD receives identity initialization while competitors receive random initialization, a consequential difference under the extremely large sparsity penalties. Results lack variability across repeated runs and ablations separating initialization, reflections, and surrogate choices. Reporting objective values alone also leaves practical PCA quality unclear; the stated runtime budget is inconsistent between the text and tables.
